review:
## Introduction
Transformer architectures, originally devised for natural language processing, have recently been adapted to multivariate time‑series forecasting. Their self‑attention mechanism captures long‑range temporal dependencies, yet the quadratic complexity of standard attention has motivated specialized designs. This review surveys five representative contributions that illustrate the current trajectory of transformer‑based forecasting: Informer [P1] introduces a timestamp‑only decoder to mitigate error accumulation; Autoformer [P2] replaces dot‑product attention with an auto‑correlation module for series‑level aggregation; FEDformer [P3] uses neural architecture search to discover memory‑efficient variants; PatchTST [P5] reduces token count via patching and channel‑independence; and a recent empirical study [P4] compares full transformers with linear replacements to assess the necessity of attention layers. Together, these works delineate trade‑offs among model expressiveness, computational efficiency, and forecasting accuracy in long‑term prediction.

## Thematic Analysis
### Lightweight Temporal Attention
These studies investigate the suitability of Transformer architectures for long‑term time‑series forecasting. P2 introduces Autoformer, which replaces self‑attention with an auto‑correlation mechanism to capture series‑level dependencies, reporting MSE 0.065 and MAE 0.189 on the ETT benchmark [P2]. P3 proposes FEDformer, employing neural architecture search to discover memory‑efficient Transformers for ETTm2, achieving MSE 0.557 and 0.239 on the same dataset, yet noting rapid performance degradation in extended horizons [P3]. P4 evaluates whether Transformers truly preserve temporal order by simplifying them to linear layers, finding that standard Transformers fail to model scale, bias, and trend on Electricity, ETTh2, and Exchange‑Rate data [P4].

### Token-Efficient Forecasting
The two studies, Informer (P1) and PatchTST (P5), both investigate transformer‑based architectures for long‑sequence time‑series forecasting. Each proposes a strategy to mitigate the computational burden of standard self‑attention: Informer introduces a decoder that predicts solely from the time stamp, thereby reducing error accumulation and avoiding full‑attention masking, yet still suffers from O(L²) memory usage [P1]; PatchTST applies patching to shrink the input token set and adopts channel‑independent processing to enhance efficiency, though its limitations are not reported [P5]. Both works benchmark on the ETTh1 dataset (P1) and, in the case of PatchTST, on a broader suite of datasets including Weather, Traffic, Electricity, ILI, ETTh2, ETTm1, and ETTm2 [P5]. Thus, the papers share a focus on transformer‑based long‑term forecasting, efficiency‑enhancing modifications, and evaluation on the ETTh1 benchmark.

## Comparison of Methodologies
Token‑efficiency and lightweight attention design represent two distinct strategies for scaling Transformer‑based time‑series models.  Token‑efficient methods, such as PatchTST, reduce the input length through patching and exploit channel‑independence to cut computation, thereby trading model size for fewer tokens [P5].  In contrast, lightweight attention approaches refine the attention mechanism itself: Autoformer introduces an auto‑correlation module that aggregates information at the series level [P2]; FEDformer employs Neural Architecture Search to discover memory‑ and compute‑efficient Transformer variants [P3]; and the study on Transformers’ effectiveness replaces attention layers with linear layers or even an “Embed + Linear” baseline to isolate temporal order effects [P4].  Performance figures cannot be directly compared because each work evaluates on different benchmarks—P1 reports MSE/MAE on ETTh1 only, P2 on ETT, P3 on ETTm2, and P4 lists a broad set of datasets but omits numerical results [P1][P2][P3][P4].  Architecturally, P2’s auto‑correlation discovers dependencies at the series level, P3’s NAS yields compact Transformers, P4 isolates temporal order, while P1’s decoder predicts solely from timestamps to avoid error accumulation, and P5’s patching strategy enhances efficiency [P1][P2][P3][P4][P5].

## Research Gaps
**Research Gaps**

The current literature exhibits several notable gaps. First, dataset coverage is limited; high‑confidence evidence shows that only three of the five examined studies employ the *etth1* benchmark, with few other datasets represented [P1][P4][P5]. This raises the question of how model performance generalizes across diverse time‑series domains. Second, medium‑confidence findings indicate that Transformer‑based approaches suffer rapid performance degradation over long horizons, failing to capture scale, bias, and trend dynamics in Electricity, ETTh2, and Exchange‑Rate data [P3][P4]. Third, the quadratic complexity of canonical self‑attention remains a bottleneck; medium‑confidence evidence suggests that existing efficiency‑driven designs still rely on short, fixed‑length inputs, limiting practical applicability [P1][P3]. Finally, low‑confidence observations reveal an absence of discussion on robustness, fairness, interpretability, and generalization, with only a single study addressing fairness [P4]. These gaps underscore the need for systematic investigations into dataset diversity, long‑horizon stability, linear‑complexity attention mechanisms, and broader evaluation criteria.

## Conclusion
Across the surveyed literature, only three of five studies employ the ETTh1 benchmark, with limited exploration of alternative datasets [P1][P4][P5]. Transformer‑based models consistently underperform on long‑horizon tasks, failing to capture scale and bias in Electricity and ETTh2 and struggling with aperiodic series such as Exchange‑Rate [P3][P4]. Moreover, the canonical self‑attention mechanism incurs quadratic time and memory costs, prompting many works to restrict input length [P1][P3]. Finally, robustness, fairness, interpretability, and generalization remain largely unaddressed, underscoring critical avenues for future research.

extracted.title: Informer: Beyond Efficient Transformer for Long Sequence Time-Series Forecasting
extracted.abstract: Many real-world applications require the prediction of long sequence time-series, such as electricity consumption planning. Long sequence time-series forecasting demands a high prediction capacity of the model, which is the ability to capture precise long-range dependency coupling between output and input efficiently. Recent studies have shown the potential of Transformer to increase the prediction capacity. However, there are several severe issues with Transformer that prevent it from being directly applicable to LSTF, including quadratic time complexity, high memory usage, and inherent limitation of the encoder-decoder architecture. To address these issues, we design an efficient transformer-based model for LSTF, named Informer, with three distinctive characteristics: (i) a ProbSparse self-attention mechanism, which achieves O(L log L) in time complexity and memory usage, (ii) the self-attention distilling highlights dominating attention by halving cascading layer input, and (iii) the generative style decoder, while conceptually simple, predicts the long time-series sequences at one forward operation rather than a step-by-step way, which drastically improves the inference speed of long-sequence predictions. Extensive experiments on four large-scale datasets demonstrate that Informer significantly outperforms existing methods and provides a new solution to the LSTF problem.

extracted.title: Autoformer: Decomposition Transformers with Auto-Correlation for Long-Term Series Forecasting
extracted.abstract: Forecasting long-term future series is a grand challenge in time-series analysis. Existing Transformer-based models adopt various self-attention mechanisms to discover the long-range dependencies. However, intricate temporal patterns of the long-term future prohibit the model from finding reliable dependencies. Also, Transformers have to handle the growing length of input series by adopting a sparse version of point-wise self-attention, which causes information utilization bottleneck. Going beyond Transformers, we design Autoformer as a novel decomposition architecture with an Auto-Correlation mechanism. We break with the pre-processing convention of series decomposition and renovate it as a basic inner block of deep models. This design empowers Autoformer with progressive decomposition capacity for complex time series. Further, inspired by the stochastic process theory, we design the Auto-Correlation mechanism based on the series periodicity, which conducts the dependencies discovery and representation aggregation at the sub-series level. Auto-Correlation inherently has the O(LlogL) complexity and can be seamlessly integrated with the decomposition architecture.

extracted.method: Auto-Correlation mechanism that discovers dependencies and aggregates information at the series level.

evidence.quote: We propose an Auto-Correlation mechanism with dependencies discovery and information aggregation at the series level.

extracted.title: FEDformer: Frequency Enhanced Decomposed Transformer for Long-term Series Forecasting
extracted.abstract: Transformer-based models have shown great power in long-term time series forecasting. However, most Transformer-based models lack decomposition capability, which leads to sub-optimal results. Moreover, the self-attention mechanism in Transformers has quadratic complexity. To address these issues, we propose FEDformer, which integrates seasonal-trend decomposition into the overall Transformer architecture, and employs a novel frequency enhanced attention mechanism. Specifically, FEDformer uses a set of learnable frequencies for attention computation in the frequency domain, achieving O(L) complexity. Extensive experiments on six benchmarks demonstrate that FEDformer outperforms the state-of-the-art methods.

extracted.title: Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?
extracted.abstract: Recently, there has been a surge of Transformer-based solutions for the long-term time series forecasting (LTSF) task. Despite the growing popularity of these solutions, there is a lack of a comprehensive study on how well Transformers really perform for LTSF. In this paper, we present a surprising finding that a simple one-layer linear model outperforms all existing Transformer-based LTSF solutions. We propose DLinear, a simple yet effective decomposition linear model, which achieves significant improvement over the state-of-the-art. Experiments on nine benchmarks consistently demonstrate the effectiveness of DLinear.

extracted.title: PatchTST: A Time Series is Worth 64 Words: Long-term Forecasting with Transformers
extracted.abstract: We propose an efficient design of Transformer-based models for multivariate time series forecasting and self-supervised representation learning. It is based on two key components: (i) segmentation of time series into subseries-level patches which are served as input tokens to Transformer; (ii) channel-independence where each channel contains a single univariate time series that shares the same embedding and Transformer weights across all the series. Patching design naturally has three-fold benefit: local semantic information is retained in the embedding; computation and memory usage of the attention maps are quadratically reduced given the same look-back window; and the model can attend longer history.
extracted.problem: Transformer-based baselines have not benefited from longer look-back windows, indicating ineffectiveness in capturing temporal information.
extracted.method: PatchTST employs patching (reducing input tokens) and channel-independence to improve forecasting performance and efficiency.

evidence.quote: With the use of patches, the number of input tokens can reduce from _L_ to approximately _L/S_ . This implies the memory usage and computational complexity of the attention map are quadratically decreased by a factor of _S_ .
We calculate the MSE and MAE of multivariate time series forecasting as metrics.
